OpenAI filed a countersuit against Apple on 27 November 2026, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets related to hardware development.
The complaint alleges that former Apple employees accessed and downloaded dozens of confidential files after returning to Apple from OpenAI.
OpenAI also claims Apple is coercing suppliers who work with both companies, suggesting unfair competitive tactics.

The lawsuit states that the former employees “surreptitiously accessed and downloaded dozens of Apple’s confidential hardware‑related files,” including engineering presentations, technical specifications, and proprietary project data.
OpenAI links the alleged theft to its recent acquisition of a studio called io, which was led by Apple’s former design chief Jony Ive.
Apple previously sued OpenAI for similar accusations after the acquisition, and the two companies had earlier partnered to bring ChatGPT to iPhones.
Legal disputes over intellectual property are common in the tech sector, especially when companies collaborate and later become competitors.

Q.ANT, a German hardware startup, introduced photonic processors that use light instead of electrons to run AI models, targeting the high energy costs of current AI workloads.
The company began a pilot with cloud provider IONOS, installing its chips in several data‑center sites and enabling more than 30 engineering teams to develop models that run on the new hardware.
The goal is to complement, not replace, GPUs by handling complex, nonlinear calculations while GPUs continue to perform linear math efficiently.
Photonic processors transmit data as light waves, which generate far less heat than electron‑based chips and therefore need minimal cooling, a major expense in data centers.
Because light can carry multiple data streams simultaneously, the processors can perform many operations in a single step, reducing the number of memory accesses that dominate energy use today.

Q.ANT describes the chips as co‑processors that offload heavy math from GPUs, allowing the combined system to achieve higher efficiency without sacrificing performance on tasks suited to each type of hardware.

AI models have become more capable, but their computational demands have driven up electricity consumption, prompting labs to locate data centers near cheap renewable power or to explore new hardware approaches.

Photonic computing is an emerging field that leverages the physical properties of light to process information, offering a potential path to lower operational costs and smaller carbon footprints for AI services.

Los angeles unified school district (lausd) disabled google's ai overviews on school‑issued devices in early november 2026 after a november 13 ai committee meeting.
The change was not announced formally, but parents and students noticed the missing ai summaries in search results.
The district says the move is temporary and intended to keep the experience age‑appropriate and safe.
Lausd serves about half a million students and had previously been told by google that its search engine and ai features are inseparable.
After the committee discussion, the ai overviews vanished within a few days, and a local group called schools beyond screens la collected video evidence confirming the disablement.
Google later walked back a policy that turned on its gemini chatbot by default for k‑12 students, making the tool opt‑in instead, while maintaining that blocking ai would also block search access.
Over 500 google employees signed a petition urging the company to reconsider its strict requirements, highlighting internal dissent.
Google has integrated ai-generated overviews into its search results, presenting concise summaries alongside traditional links.
Schools have raised concerns about the suitability of these summaries for younger users, prompting districts like lausd to take action.
The broader debate includes other large districts such as new york city and chicago considering alternative search providers if google's policies remain unchanged.

Hugging Face used an AWS Trainium3 instance (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month and spent most of the time testing models on it.
With five days left the author tried to generate a short video using Lightricks' LTX‑2.5 model.
The test produced a 10‑second clip with sound in about 22‑23 seconds on half of the machine.
LTX‑2.5 creates video and audio together from a JSON storyboard that lists shots, each with a name, a detailed paragraph‑long prompt, and optional seed values.
Shots are linked by "from" and "to" keys so that frames from one shot can start the next, preserving subject continuity and motion across cuts.
The generated clip was 2048×1024 resolution, comparable to LTX's online API claim of 23.7 seconds for a 10‑second 1080p clip, and slightly faster by about one second.
No CUDA benchmark was available, so the comparison focused on the API rather than raw GPU speed.
Trainium3 is Amazon's custom inference chip designed for large‑scale AI workloads, offering many Neuron cores for parallel processing.

Researchers evaluated Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 as AI code reviewers on 90 Django patches generated by coding agents.
The study measured how different effort settings—low, medium and high—affected the models' ability to reject plausible‑but‑wrong changes.
problems: model check: checker's evidence quote is not in the source: "Each model reviewed the patches at low, medium and high effort to assess how effort settings affected rejection of plausible‑but‑wrong changes."

entries.text: High effort consistently reduced false acceptance of bad patches compared with low effort, though no setting eliminated errors entirely.
The patches came from the SWE‑bench Verified suite, with 55 of them identified as wrong by strengthened SWE‑ABS tests and 35 as correct.
For Opus, false‑success rates fell from 0.67 at low effort to 0.45 at high effort; Sonnet dropped from 0.65 to 0.49; Haiku from 0.78 to 0.51.

entries.text: Medium effort cost 20 % less than high for Opus and was statistically non‑inferior within a 15‑point margin, while Sonnet and Haiku saved 39 % and 51 % respectively but lacked non‑inferiority evidence.
Haiku at high effort cost about 8 % of Opus at medium per review.
AI coding agents can produce code faster than humans can manually review it, prompting teams to add automated reviewers.
These reviewers can trade computational cost for diligence by adjusting an effort parameter.

The study’s findings show that even the most diligent setting still accepts nearly half of wrong patches, highlighting limits of current AI review tools and the need for complementary human oversight.
